doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Becoming a professional musician
summary: Great Lakes and then Parker convinced him to be a professional; he learned Goodman and Shaw from mail-order music and radio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: So playing on a bandstand for people started when you were in college.
Right.
First couple of years.
Mmm-hmm.

The implication I got from the story you told about Great Lakes, where you peeked in and the bandmaster discovered you could play clarinet well... I’m interested in how you went from being a student to the idea that you were going to be a professional musician, how that
crystallized in you.
Well, once I heard the band at Great Lakes, I wanted to be a professional musician. Up until then, I hadn’t really thought about it.
So that made you think “this is what I want to do.”
Yes, that’s exactly what I want to do. After I heard Charlie Parker, that really solidified.
But before that, you were talking about practicing the Benny Goodman solos.
Yes.
Did you practice to a lot of clarinet players when you were 14-15-16?
Oh, no-no, no-no. It was just me. I’d send to New York and get his music...
The transcribed solos.
Transcribed. And Artie Shaw. People like that.
But had you listened to Benny Goodman or Artie Shaw by that time?

Oh, yeah. I listened to them. I listened to them on radio. I told you we had a short­ wave radio. We could pick it up late at night down in the South. We’d pick them up. When they got to 12 o’clock, we couldn’t...
I wasn’t sure of the timeline, whether that was before the war or after the war that you were able to do that.
that was during the war.
Of course. You were 15 when the war started. But what I meant to say was, before you were drafted.
No, that wasn’t before then.
